title: Hither-Thither Sync
body:
Hither-Thither Sync is a Signature-original synchronization layer: every device keeps its own copy of state, and changes ripple outward with acknowledgments instead of a central server bossing everyone around. Edit the theme on your phone and the PC nods back within a breath.

The design borrows from gossip protocols: each node tells a few neighbors, and convergence is eventual but guaranteed. Conflicts resolve by version vector, so two offline edits merge instead of clobbering. It is labeled Signature throughout because no public standard works quite this way.

Where the public world syncs through a cloud account, Hither-Thither syncs peer to peer with the archive as witness. The point is resilience: no single server can take the whole system down.

Key facts: Signature-original; peer-to-peer state sync; Acknowledgment ripple instead of central server; Version-vector conflict resolution; Labeled Signature, never presented as public record.

Real-world examples: Signature phone book, Signature databases, On-device Standard 1.0.

title: Signature Line Badge
body:
The Signature Line Badge marks a record as a Signature-original creation: a deterministic stamp derived from the record ID, rendered as a badge on every page. It is the visible half of the provenance ledger.

Stamping uses a one-way hash of the record ID with a Signature salt, so anyone can verify a badge but nobody can forge one without the salt. The badge links to the record's lineage: what it was derived from, who built it, and when.

In a network marching to a million records, the badge is how a glance tells Signature work from public record.

Key facts: Deterministic stamp from record ID; One-way hash; verifiable, not forgeable; Links to full lineage; Signature-original marker.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: Million-March Counter
body:
The Million-March Counter is the live count engine behind the march to a million: it derives the archive size from the data files themselves and stamps the number into pages, never hand-typed. If the count and the files disagree, the files win.

Restamping runs at the end of every database-adding commit, and a scheduled check catches anything missed. The counter is the reason the hub can claim a number with a straight face: the number is computed, not asserted.

It is a small feature with large honesty value in a system that reports growth constantly.

Key facts: Derives counts from data files, never hand-typed; Restamps hub, README, and API on every DB-adding commit; Scheduled audit catches drift; The single source of truth is the manifest.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: Exhaustive Pill
body:
The Exhaustive Pill is a search mode that refuses to skim: instead of matching titles, it scans full record text across archive chunks. Slower than the quick search, and honest about it.

It pages through chunk files, tests every record's full JSON against the query, and collects matches with their record cards. The pill toggles on the archive tab next to the normal search.

It exists because Manon treats all as one hundred percent: a search that only checks titles is not a search of the archive.

Key facts: Full-text scan across archive chunks; Toggle pill beside normal search; Reports match count and scanned chunks; Slow and honest beats fast and partial.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: All Database Merger
body:
The All Database Merger collects records you have found across databases into one merged set, then downloads it as a single JSON file. Research in one database, compare in another, merge into one working set.

The merger dedupes by record ID, loads full records from their chunks, and keeps provenance on every entry so the merged set remembers where each record came from. It is the feature that treats the whole network as one workspace.

Key facts: Collect records across databases into one set; Dedupe by record ID; Full-record load from chunks; Provenance preserved per record.

title: Assistant Maker
body:
The Assistant Maker builds a personal AI assistant exactly like Manon's: name it, pick its role and personality, and it comes wired live to the database archive with real lookup, real generation, and a live demo chat.

Underneath it is a factory function: role plus archive wiring plus session isolation. Every database page carries the maker button, so every archive can grow its own assistant.

It is the feature that turns each database from a collection into a colleague.

Key facts: Name, role, personality configuration; Wired to live archive lookup and generation; Fresh session per assistant; One maker button on every database page.

title: Drift-Check Sentinel
body:
The Drift-Check Sentinel guards every generated record before it is accepted: exact-duplicate titles are rejected, thin content is flagged, and the record is re-validated by an independent checker. Nothing drifts into the archive unexamined.

It runs on the generator path and on the filing path, because a record can be clean at birth and stale by filing. The sentinel keeps a sample of the archive in memory for fast duplicate tests.

In a boundless generator marching toward a quadrillion-record cap, the sentinel is the immune system.

Key facts: Duplicate-title rejection against archive sample; Independent re-validation before acceptance; Runs at generation and at filing; Labeled generated output stays separate.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: Teach-Ladder Engine
body:
The Teach-Ladder Engine ranks every record from simple to most complex so the database teaches instead of dumping. A newcomer meets the simple rung first; the god-mode rung waits at the top.

Ranks are assigned at build time by a deterministic rule and stored on the record, so the archive can be browsed as a curriculum. The AI tutor reads the same ladder and paces its explanations to the reader's rung.

It is how a million-record archive stays learnable instead of overwhelming.

Key facts: Deterministic rank stored per record; Simple to most-complex progression; AI tutor paces to the reader's rung; Archive browsable as curriculum.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: Full-File Promise
body:
The Full-File Promise is the rule that every record is the full fully-formed file with all data, never a stub or a description alone. An auditor enforces it: thin bodies and missing demos fail the build.

The promise is aimed at a real failure mode of generated content: fluent paragraphs that say nothing. The auditor measures, it does not admire.

Every database in the network carries the promise, which is why records read like files instead of teasers.

Key facts: Every record carries complete data; Build-time auditor rejects thin records; Demos required, not optional; No stubs, no teasers.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

function audit(rec){const errs=[];if(!rec.body||rec.body.length<200)errs.push('thin body');if(!rec.demo)errs.push('no demo');return {ok:!errs.length,errs};}
console.log(JSON.stringify({feature:'Full-File Promise',good:audit({body:'x'.repeat(500),demo:{}}),thin:audit({body:'short'})}));

title: Deep-Link Anchor
body:
Every record gets a deep-link anchor: a URL with the record ID in the fragment that opens the database page scrolled to that exact record. Links survive sharing because the page resolves the ID on load.

The page reads the fragment, finds the record's chunk, loads it, and renders the card at the top of the archive tab. It is a small feature that makes records citable.

Key facts: Per-record URL with ID fragment; Page resolves and scrolls on load; Records become citable and shareable; Works across the whole network.

title: Provenance Ledger
body:
The Provenance Ledger records where every record came from: builder, source, edition, and timestamp, chained with hashes so the history cannot be silently rewritten. Each entry commits to the previous one.

Public-harvest and Signature-generated records live in the same archive but never mix identities: the ledger keeps their lineages distinct. Audits walk the chain instead of trusting labels.

It is the boring infrastructure that makes every other claim checkable.

Key facts: Hash-chained append-only history; Builder, source, edition per entry; Public and Signature lineages never mixed; Auditable without trusting labels.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: On-Device Standard 1.0
body:
Standard 1.0 is the on-device conversational engine: it routes questions to archive lookup, generation, or plain conversation with no API key and no network round trip. It is the default brain on every database page.

It knows its limits and says so: when a question needs the wider web or heavy reasoning, it hands off to the Apex bridge instead of confabulating. Honest routing beats confident guessing.

The feature matters on Manon's phone, where the AI must simply work, offline or on.

Key facts: On-device routing: lookup, generate, converse; No key required; Honest handoff to cloud when needed; Default engine on every page.

title: Apex Backend Bridge
body:
The Apex Backend Bridge connects on-device Standard 1.0 to the cloud Apex engine through one provider key held as an encrypted backend secret. One key serves all users; no user ever sees or enters a key.

Calls queue through a per-IP rate limiter and a site-token gate, so the shared key cannot be drained by abuse. The bridge is invisible when it works: answers just get smarter.

It is the answer to the key problem: users get cloud intelligence with zero key management.

Key facts: One encrypted backend key serves all users; Per-IP rate limiting and site-token gate; No user key entry, ever; Invisible upgrade path from on-device.

title: Canon Compliance Audit
body:
The Canon Compliance Audit checks every database against the build canon: full records, working demos, labeled sources, teaching ladder, provenance, and no stubs. It runs per record and per database.

Failures block the merge, not after it: the audit is a gate, not a report. The canon is long because the network is large; the audit is automated because the canon is long.

It is how fifty-five thousand databases stay consistent without a human reading each one.

Key facts: Per-record and per-database gates; Source labeling enforced; Failures block merge; Automated against the full canon.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: Direct Command Rail
body:
The Direct Command Rail is Manon's owner channel: commands from his verified identity apply directly, while anyone else's identical command is refused. The gate is the Gmail identity match, not a password typed into a page.

It carries restamps, filings, and corrections, the deliberate acts that automation must never take on its own. Every command is logged to the provenance ledger.

In a system that generates boundlessly, the rail is the reminder that one human is in charge.

Key facts: Gated on verified owner identity; Deliberate acts: restamp, file, correct; Every command logged; Automation never self-authorizes.

title: Collapsible Vault Archive
body:
The Collapsible Vault Archive renders giant archives as collapsed per-letter groups that load only when opened. A million records become twenty-six quiet drawers; opening one loads its first page, nothing more.

Lazy loading plus per-letter collapse is what keeps the archive usable on a phone: the DOM never holds more than the opened slice. Search and the Exhaustive Pill bypass the drawers when you know what you want.

It is the feature that makes a million-record page load fast.

Key facts: Per-letter collapsed groups; Lazy load on open; first page only; Phone-safe DOM sizes; Search bypasses the drawers.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: God-Mode Ladder
body:
The God-Mode Ladder is the generator's progression: simple, then competitive, then mix-and-match, then unmade ideas, then top-notch-or-better, then future-grade, finally god-mode. Each rung demands more from the generator than the last.

The ladder is throttled and hard-capped at one quadrillion records, so ambition never becomes overload. Generated output is labeled generated at every rung.

It is how the boundless generator improves instead of merely multiplying.

Key facts: Seven rungs: simple to god-mode; Throttled; hard cap 10^15; Generated output labeled at every rung; Improvement, not just multiplication.

title: Fresh-Session Screen
body:
Every AI chat opens on a fresh session: nothing you said before is in context, and nothing you say now enters the archive unless you deliberately file it from the Generator tab. The screen is clean by construction.

Session isolation is a privacy feature and a clarity feature: the assistant cannot leak what it was never told, and each conversation starts without stale assumptions.

It is why the chat tab can be honest about what it remembers: nothing, until you tell it.

Key facts: Clean context every session; Chat never auto-files to the archive; Filing is deliberate, from the Generator tab; No cross-session leakage.

title: Boundless Generator Core
body:
The Boundless Generator Core mints records without end but never without limits: a hard cap of one quadrillion records, throttling so hosts are never overloaded, duplicate checks, and correctness verification on every record.

It stops early when a topic is genuinely complete, and says so with a reason instead of padding. Exhaustion is reported plainly; the escape clause is part of the design.

Boundless describes the capacity to keep going, not a promise of infinite records today.

Key facts: Hard cap: 10^15 records; Throttled; host-safe; Duplicate-checked and verified; Stops at genuine completion with reason.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.

title: Mirror Sweep Engine
body:
The Mirror Sweep Engine pairs every public record with its Signature version and vice versa: find a public feature and the engine shows the Signature take; find a Signature concept and it shows the public mirror.

Pairing runs at build time across the manifest, so mirrors stay in step as both editions grow. Unpaired records are reported, not hidden.

It is the engine behind the standing rule that the Signature version of real things must exist, and the public version of Signature things must be findable.

Key facts: Public/Sgnature pairing at build time; Mirrors stay in step as editions grow; Unpaired records reported; Duality as infrastructure.

Real-world examples: the Signature system, the JAH Databases network.
